Before diving into the different meanings, here's the unifying idea that runs through all of them: runoff is what happens when a system reaches its limit and the excess spills over or flows away. Keep this in mind — it makes every meaning feel intuitive.
Meaning 1: Water That Flows Over Land (The Primary Meaning)

This is the most widely used meaning, especially in science, environment, and everyday conversation.

When rain falls or snow melts, the earth can only absorb so much water. Think of the soil like a sponge — a sponge can hold a certain amount of liquid, but once it's full, any extra liquid just runs right off it. The water that the ground cannot soak in starts flowing across the surface — over roads, fields, rooftops, hillsides, and parking lots — until it eventually reaches a stream, river, lake, or the ocean.

That excess water flowing across the surface of the land is called runoff.

Example: After a heavy storm, you can literally see runoff — the water streaming across the road, rushing down gutters, or flowing through ditches.

Why Runoff Matters

Understanding runoff is not just a geography lesson — it has real consequences:

Flooding. When there is too much runoff and water bodies cannot absorb it fast enough, the excess water overflows onto land. Cities pave over natural soil, which means rain has fewer places to soak in, so urban areas often experience heavy runoff and are more flood-prone.

Pollution. As runoff flows across the land, it picks up whatever it passes over — fertilizers from farms, oil and grease from roads, pesticides from gardens, animal waste, industrial chemicals. It carries all of this into rivers and lakes. This is why you'll often hear the phrases:

  • Agricultural runoff — water carrying fertilizers and pesticides from farmland into rivers, often causing excessive algae growth in lakes (called eutrophication).
  • Urban runoff — water flowing off city roads and rooftops, carrying pollutants into local waterways.
  • Stormwater runoff — a broader term for all the water generated by rain events that flows off surfaces rather than soaking in.

Erosion. Runoff physically moves soil particles as it flows. Over time, this strips away the top layer of soil (the most fertile layer), damages hillsides, and silts up rivers.

Drought and water supply. Ironically, too much runoff can contribute to drought. If water rushes away as runoff instead of soaking into the ground, it doesn't replenish groundwater reserves, which are what wells and springs depend on.

The Water Cycle Connection

Runoff is a key part of the water cycle. Rain falls → some evaporates, some soaks into the ground, and the rest becomes runoff → runoff flows into rivers and oceans → water evaporates from those bodies → it forms clouds → it rains again.

The second major meaning is completely different in subject but follows the same logic: what happens when no clear outcome is reached in the first attempt.

A runoff (also called a runoff election) is a second round of voting held because the first election did not produce a winner who meets the required threshold — usually an outright majority (more than 50% of the votes).

Here's why it happens:

Imagine an election with three candidates:

  • Candidate A gets 40% of the votes
  • Candidate B gets 35% of the votes
  • Candidate C gets 25% of the votes

Candidate A won the most votes, but not a majority — more than half of voters preferred someone else. Many electoral systems require a winner to have majority support, not just more votes than the others. So the election is unresolved after the first round.

A runoff is then held between the top two finishers (A and B in this case). Voters now choose between just those two candidates, so one of them must get a majority. The runoff produces a clear, decisive winner.

Example sentences:

  • "No candidate crossed the 50% threshold, so the race will go to a runoff next month."
  • "The two candidates who advanced to the runoff spent weeks campaigning intensively."

Runoff elections are common in many countries, U.S. Senate and gubernatorial races in some states (notably Georgia), and local elections. The specific rules vary — some systems require exactly 50%+1 to avoid a runoff; others set a different threshold.
Meaning 3: Overflow or Leftover in a Process (Specialized/Technical)

In industrial, manufacturing, and financial contexts, runoff can refer to the leftover, overflow, or gradual tail-end of a process — what remains after the main activity is complete.

  • In manufacturing, runoff can describe excess material (like molten metal or paint) that overflows or drips away during production.
  • In finance and insurance, a "runoff" refers to a situation where a company stops taking on new business but continues managing its existing obligations until they are all settled — like a gradual winding-down. An insurance company in runoff, for instance, is still paying out old claims but not issuing new policies.
  • More generally, "runoff" can describe any gradual diminishment — the slow expiration of a portfolio, contracts, or liabilities over time.

This usage is technical and context-specific. You'll mostly encounter it in finance, insurance, and industrial settings.

The word "runoff" always carries the idea of excess flowing away, spilling over, or what happens after the main capacity is used up.

ContextWhat "runs off"
Water & environmentRain that the ground can't absorb
ElectionsVotes that didn't decide a winner in round one
Finance/industryObligations or material that remain after the main process ends

If you want to remember this word in its most important sense: Runoff is what flows away when something can't hold any more. Water runs off land. Votes "run over" into a second election. Obligations run off slowly at the tail end of a business.

That's runoff — completely and accurately explained.
